title: Build Image on Host
summary: Adversaries build a container image directly on a compromised host to avoid pulling a known malicious image from a public registry. A build request sent to the container runtime API carries instructions that start from an ordinary base image, fetch extra content, and produce a new image stored locally on that host. Because the base is a common distribution image that defenders expect to see, registry scanning and image reputation checks have nothing suspicious to report. The resulting image is then used to start containers that run the attacker's code. Pulling the base from a local registry is quieter still, since those layers already exist inside the environment. Detection depends less on image reputation and more on build events in the runtime API, outbound network connections made during the build, and container images that exist on a host with no matching registry record.

beginner.definition: A container image is a packaged set of files used to start containers. Normally images come from an online library called a registry. An attacker can instead build a new image on a machine they already control. That way no suspicious image is ever downloaded from outside.
beginner.whyItMatters: Many teams trust images that come from well known public sources. Building locally avoids those checks completely, because the starting point is a normal image. The finished image never leaves the host, so a registry scan will not see it. Without host level build logs, this activity is easy to miss.
howItWorks: The attacker already has access to a host that runs container software.
They send a build request to the container service running on that host.
The request starts from a normal public image, so nothing looks suspicious.
During the build, extra files and programs are added to the new image.
The image is stored locally, so tools that watch downloads see nothing.
The attacker then starts a container from that local image to run their code.
beginner.example: Think of an office with a photocopier in the corner. Everyone is used to seeing paper come out of it, so nobody watches the machine itself. A visitor brings in their own pages, copies them onto the office paper, and leaves with a stack that matches the office style exactly. The paper tray was never empty and the machine never broke. The only odd thing was that somebody used the copier when no printing job was expected.
takeaways: A locally built image can carry malicious content while looking ordinary.
Defences that only check downloaded images will not see this.
Build events on container hosts are a key source of evidence.

objectives: Explain why building an image locally avoids registry based defences.
Describe how a vanilla base image can be used to hide a custom image.
Identify the API activity that indicates an image build on a host.
Explain how outbound connections during a build reveal malicious content retrieval.
Summarise how local images can be detected without registry visibility.
